```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

Calculating ages and putting them into useful groups are everyday tasks in
many disciplines, from public health and education to population research.
A birth date and an event date look simple enough, but birthdays, leap years,
time units, and group boundaries can make the details surprisingly fiddly.

**agecraft** brings those steps together in a flexible, vector-based framework:
calculate ages, keep track of their units, and classify them into groups you
can use in tables and analyses. This introduction walks through that workflow
using ordinary R vectors and data frames.

## Load the package

Once agecraft is installed, load it with:

```{r load-package}
library(agecraft)
```

The main functions we will use are `calculate_age()` and `categorize_age()`.

## Meet the age class

An R class tells R what a value represents and how it should behave. The
package's S3 class, `age`, represents an age with a time unit. You do not need
to understand class programming to use it.

An `age` vector can:

- Store fractional ages without discarding their precision.
- Display completed whole units, as people usually report their age.
- Keep one unit, such as year, month, week, or day, for the entire vector.
- Retain its unit when you select, sort, or combine observations.
- Supply its stored fractional values when you classify ages into groups.

For a small example, construct an age directly:

```{r meet-age}
example_age <- age(2.75, unit = "year")
example_age
as.numeric(example_age)
as.integer(example_age)
```

The printed age is `2 year`, but the stored value is **2.75 years**.
`as.numeric()` extracts the fractional value; `as.integer()` extracts the
completed whole units. Printing the age does not round or change its value.
To display the fractions explicitly, use:

```{r show-fractions}
format(example_age, fractional = TRUE)
```

## Calculate ages from dates

Most workflows start with dates rather than numeric ages. `calculate_age()`
needs a `start`, usually a birth date. Its `end` is the date or time at which
you want to know the age. R needs these as dates or date-times, rather than
ordinary text, so use `as.Date()` for calendar dates.

### Age on a reference date

Here are three birth dates and a single reference date:

```{r reference-date}
birth_dates <- as.Date(c("2024-01-01", "2022-01-01", "2020-01-01"))
reference_date <- as.Date("2024-07-02")

ages <- calculate_age(start = birth_dates, end = reference_date)
ages
```

The default unit is **year**, and the default result is an `age` vector.
One reference date is reused for every birth date. There is no need to write
a loop. This example uses a fixed reference date so its results are reproducible.

### Age today

To calculate ages as of today, supply today's date:

```{r today}
calculate_age(start = birth_dates, end = Sys.Date())
```

You can also omit `end` entirely: `calculate_age(start = birth_dates)` uses
the current date-time. Results based on today naturally change over time.

### Age at an event

For age at a visit, enrollment, or another event, give each observation its
own event date. The birth dates and event dates should have the same length,
or one of the two vectors must have length one.

```{r event-dates}
event_dates <- as.Date(c("2024-02-01", "2024-08-01", "2024-09-01"))
ages_at_event <- calculate_age(start = birth_dates, end = event_dates)

data.frame(birth_date = birth_dates, event_date = event_dates,
           age_at_event = ages_at_event)
```

An event must not precede the corresponding birth date. Missing dates produce
missing ages rather than removing observations.

### Choose a unit

Use `unit` to ask for years, months, weeks, days, hours, minutes, or seconds.
The argument uses singular names:

```{r choose-unit}
calculate_age(birth_dates, reference_date, unit = "month")
calculate_age(birth_dates, reference_date, unit = "day")
```

Years and months use calendar anniversaries. A fractional year is the number
of completed birthdays plus the fraction of days between the previous and
next birthdays. Months use the analogous month anniversaries. Leap birthdays
fall on March 1 in non-leap years; month anniversaries fall on the last day of
a shorter month when necessary.

For date-times, calendar years and months use civil dates in the starting
time zone and ignore time of day. Smaller units measure elapsed time: a day
means 24 hours, so crossing a daylight-saving transition may give a fraction
of a day.

## Choose what calculate_age returns

`calculate_age()` offers three output formats:

| `output` | Returned object | Values stored |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `"age"` (default) | An `age` vector with a unit | Fractional ages; completed units displayed |
| `"units"` | A vector from the units package | Completed whole units, with a unit |
| `"numeric"` | A plain numeric vector | Completed whole units, without a unit |

```{r output-options}
calculate_age(birth_dates, reference_date, output = "age")
calculate_age(birth_dates, reference_date, output = "units")
calculate_age(birth_dates, reference_date, output = "numeric")
```

There is an important distinction between requesting plain numeric output
and extracting numbers from an `age` object:

```{r extraction}
as.numeric(ages) # fractional values, with the class and unit removed
as.integer(ages) # completed whole units
```

Use the default `age` output when you want to retain fractions for later
classification. `output = "units"` preserves the completed-age format returned
by earlier development versions of agecraft.

## Group ages using the supplied definitions

The package includes ready-to-use cut points in `age_group_presets`. Start by
looking at their names, then select a definition:

```{r supplied-groups}
names(age_group_presets)
reporting_groups <- as.age_group(age_group_presets$Yr.5, unit = "year")
head(reporting_groups)

categories <- categorize_age(ages, by = reporting_groups)
categories
table(categories)
```

`as.age_group()` turns the cut points into an `age_group` vector. Here we
explicitly say that the supplied cut points represent years. Choose a
definition that fits your analysis; the presets are inherited reporting
conventions, and their names and provenance are documented in the package.

`categorize_age()` returns an **ordered factor**: a vector of category labels
whose levels follow interval order. You can put it straight into `table()`
or add it to a data frame.

## Make and name your own groups

Suppose you want categories called Infant, Toddler, and Young child.
Construct the interval boundaries, then give each interval a name:

```{r named-groups}
child_groups <- age_group(start = c(0, 1, 3), end = c(1, 3, 6), unit = "year")
child_groups
names(child_groups) <- c("Infant", "Toddler", "Young child")

child_category <- categorize_age(ages, by = child_groups)
child_category
```

Each interval **includes its start and excludes its end**. The toddler group,
`[1, 3)`, starts on the first birthday and ends just before the third birthday.
The ordinary interval display is `1-2`, meaning completed ages 1 and 2.
If you want completed ages 1 through 3, use `[1, 4)` instead.
These labels and boundaries are examples; choose definitions for your use case.

The group names become the labels in the classified result, and they carry
through to a frequency table:

```{r named-table}
table(child_category)

data.frame(birth_date = birth_dates, age = ages, category = child_category)
```

Without names, the categories display interval labels such as `1-2`.
Missing or blank names fall back to those interval labels. Give distinct
intervals unique labels so that separate categories stay distinguishable.

### Fractional boundaries for finer categories

Groups can also have fractional boundaries. For example, you could split the
first year into an approximate neonatal period and later infancy:

```{r fractional-groups}
fine_groups <- age_group(start = c(0, 0.077, 1, 3),
                         end = c(0.077, 1, 3, 6), unit = "year")
names(fine_groups) <- c("Neonate", "Infant", "Toddler", "Young child")

fine_ages <- calculate_age(as.Date("2024-01-01"),
                          as.Date(c("2024-01-10", "2024-07-02", "2025-01-01")))
fine_category <- categorize_age(fine_ages, by = fine_groups)
fine_category
table(fine_category)
```

Classification uses the stored fractions, even when both a neonatal age and
an infant age print as `0 year`. The cutoff `0.077` years approximates 28 days;
it is not an exact calendar-day boundary. If an exact 28-day cutoff matters,
calculate the ages in days and define groups in days.

Keep groups non-overlapping when each person should belong to one category.
An age outside all intervals, or a missing age, returns `NA`. Overlapping
matches raise an error by default, helping you spot ambiguous definitions.

## Convert units explicitly

For an existing age vector, use `as_age()` to change units:

```{r convert-units}
weeks <- age(c(1.5, 2), unit = "week")
as_age(weeks, unit = "day")
```

Weeks convert to days exactly. Converting years or months to days is
approximate because calendar years and months vary in length. You must opt
in to that approximation:

```{r approximate-conversion}
approximate_days <- as_age(example_age, unit = "day", allow_approx = TRUE)
approximate_days
as.numeric(approximate_days)
```

After conversion, the fractional part is a fraction of the **new** unit.
For exact elapsed days from dates, calculate directly in days instead of
converting a fractional age in years.

## A workflow to take away

Keep the dates, calculate ages in the unit your analysis needs, and pass the
result directly to `categorize_age()`. Supply an existing group definition
or create your own intervals and names. The resulting ordered factor is
ready for a table, a plot, or the next step in your analysis.
